Slide 10 · Notes

Dentists use nitrous mixed with oxygen, for minutes, with someone watching. Balloons are pure gas, often dozens a night. Nitrous knocks out B12, which nerves need to keep their coating in repair. Seven of 20 patients in one series couldn’t walk when they arrived. Ask: why might someone ignore tingling toes for weeks?

Slide 13 · Notes

The chemicals make the heart oversensitive to adrenaline, so a scare or a chase can set off a fatal rhythm. Every hit also cuts oxygen to the brain, and the gas comes out cold enough to freeze lips and throat.

Slide 14 · Notes

Some adults use kratom for pain or to cut back on opioids, and the research is limited. If someone in a student’s family does, the safest step is talking it through with a doctor, not judging them.

Slide 15 · Notes

Small groups: five minutes to list, five to write an honest label. “Natural” and “legal” are sales words. “Lab tested” doesn’t say for what. “Not for human consumption” usually means “we don’t want to be responsible.”

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain how nitrous damages nerves, why inhalants can stop a heart, and what kratom, 7-OH and tianeptine actually are. They practice reading past product marketing. Students whose family members use kratom for pain should feel respected.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards for the exit card
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minMyth or fact, one per slide
  2. 7 minFrom balloon to numb feet, and the ER guess
  3. 4 minDusters and the heart
  4. 6 minBehind the counter
  5. 9 minTake apart the package, write an honest label
  6. 4 minWhy do these words work? Turn and talk, share out
  7. 6 minThree moments: Cole, Megan, Jordan
  8. 4 minEvery student, exit card

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Two myths, the nitrous chain, dusters and the heart, the package, and the exit card.

Before you teach
Keep it about products and claims.

This lesson works as media literacy. Ask what the package wants you to believe, not who has tried it.

Respect family members who use kratom.

Some adults use it to manage pain or cut back on opioids, and the research on that is limited. The safest step is talking it through with a doctor. Never make that adult sound foolish.

Give the nerve warning plainly.

Numbness, tingling, or weak or clumsy legs after nitrous means see a doctor soon. A normal B12 test doesn't rule out damage. Say it twice.

Teach "keep them sitting."

Most inhalant injuries happen when people stand, faint and fall. Startling or chasing someone who's been sniffing can trigger a fatal heart rhythm.

Know the 911 signs.

Won't wake up, slow or no breathing, blue lips, a seizure, chest pain, or a head injury. With kratom, 7-OH or tianeptine, give naloxone if you have it.

If a student says they can't stop.

Needing more, or feeling sick without it, is dependence. Thank them and connect them with the nurse or a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Family use for pain or recovery.

Kratom may be how a family member manages chronic pain or stays off pain pills. Students may feel protective. Keep the message "talk to a doctor" and leave the judgment out.

Work and money.

Kratom shots get sold for getting through a double shift. Some students work long hours to help their families. Name the pressure as real while explaining the product.

Where products are sold.

Smoke shops and gas stations cluster in some neighborhoods more than others. Talk about the marketing, not the neighborhood or the people who shop there.

Culture and plant medicine.

Kratom is a traditional plant in parts of Southeast Asia. Separate the plant's history from concentrated lab products like 7-OH.

Language on labels.

For students or families who read English as a second language, "botanical" and "not for human consumption" may be confusing. Plain-language rewrites help everyone.

Mixed names and situations.

Use the scenario names as written, and include coworkers and family as well as friends.

What the research says

Michigan saw 60 emergency room visits for nitrous oxide misuse in 2023, up from 7 in 2019. EMS calls rose from 15 to 78.

Vohra et al., CDC MMWR, 2025

20 patients with nerve damage from nitrous (average age 24) all had spinal cord damage on MRI, seven couldn't walk on arrival, and their average B12 test looked normal.

Swart et al., European Journal of Neurology, 2021

110 sudden deaths in young people who sniffed solvents and aerosols led to the term "sudden sniffing death"; the chemicals make the heart oversensitive to adrenaline.

Bass, JAMA, 1970

17 people had severe illness after tianeptine products, mostly Neptune's Fix. Thirteen went to intensive care, seven needed a breathing tube, and the product held synthetic cannabinoids not on the label.

Counts et al., CDC MMWR, 2024

The FDA warned people not to inhale flavored nitrous products like Galaxy Gas in March 2025, after a rise in injury reports.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2025

In July 2025 the FDA recommended making 7-OH, a concentrated kratom chemical that binds the same receptors as morphine, a controlled substance.
